tradition.name: Ambient lo-fi
tradition.lineage: An internet-circulated ambient discovery cluster whose indexed Every Noise roster includes Borrtex, Gibran Alcocer, reidenshi and SymphoCat. Documented members span quiet piano, electronic synthesis and field-recorded work. The selected piano-and-synth arrangement follows Borrtex’s mixed keyboard/electronic branch, without treating all ambient music with low fidelity as this category.

extras.description: A slow ambient listening cluster with quiet recurring figures and spatially dispersed textures. Borrtex documents electronic synthesizers with piano and other keyboards on FLUX; Alcocer’s Idea 10 documents the solo-piano branch, while SymphoCat credits field recordings. This default selects softly sustained synthesis and restrained repeating piano. Lo-fi surface treatment and environmental recordings remain optional; a cassette edition does not establish four-track recording, and no foreground beat is required by this authored arrangement.

entries.geo_rationale: Borrtex’s own Bandcamp profile identifies a Prague-based composer and pianist. These city-center coordinates anchor one verified member’s practice; they do not identify the origin of the online category or a private studio.

tradition.name: Ambient trance
tradition.lineage: The atmospheric listening side of trance and related electronic music, represented by Carbon Based Lifeforms, Solar Fields and the Ultimae orbit. Long melodic layers and repeated sequencer/bass figures may carry soft beats or become beatless. The selected model retains a measured machine pulse rather than prescribing a peak-time trance build.

extras.description: Ambient trance is an atmospheric trance-adjacent listening category, spanning hypnotic electronic sequences, resonant bass and lingering melodic layers rather than only festival-speed four-on-the-floor anthems. The source-linked Sounds of Spotify list includes Carbon Based Lifeforms, Solar Fields, AES Dana and Union Jack. The default models a gently persistent synth/bass/drum pulse. Compared with classic or uplifting trance it recesses intensity and climactic song architecture; compared with beatless ambient it retains sequenced rhythmic recurrence. There is substantial overlap with existing ambient_psychill: this allocation is a broader discovery category, not an assertion of an unrelated lineage or a uniquely measured sonic boundary.
exemplars: Solar Fields — Until We Meet the Sky

tradition.name: Ambient worship
tradition.lineage: Contemporary Christian music for prayer and reflection that uses ambient soundscapes, intimate sung phrases and melodic acoustic or electronic layers. Salt of the Sound explicitly uses this name for a listening-oriented form alongside, rather than exclusively inside, congregational worship services.

extras.description: Ambient worship places Christian prayer, hymns and reflective sung phrases within expansive soundscapes. Salt of the Sound’s firsthand definition includes both large textures and soft intimate songs, with vocals in varying amounts, and distinguishes the style from a typical Sunday congregational set. Their release notes document muted piano and ethereal phrases as well as instrumental meditations. The default is the quiet vocal/piano/pad branch, not a claim that all releases use this exact trio. Compared with contemporary_worship, drums, massed congregation and the auditorium crescendo cease to be default chairs; compared with secular ambient, the reflective Christian song function is explicit.
exemplars: Salt of the Sound — Beyond Here
Salt of the Sound — Lent, Vol. 3
Salt of the Sound & Khamir Music — words unspoken

entries.geo_rationale: Salt of the Sound’s own current biography and release pages identify Hong Kong; a documented current practice anchor, not the genre’s exclusive birthplace.

tradition.name: Argentine ambient
tradition.lineage: A geographically grouped ambient scene with multiple practices, including Leandro Fresco’s layered synthesizer compositions and Federico Durand’s intimate recorded loops and small sounds. This representative model combines quiet synth colour, a clean guitar fragment and looping recorded material; it does not assert a national timbre or compulsory tango instrumentation.

extras.description: Argentine ambient is a regional discovery category, not one inherited rhythmic form. Leandro Fresco’s El Reino Invisible documents slow synth textures and guitar details recorded between Buenos Aires and San Martín de los Andes; Federico Durand describes cassette collage, asymmetrical repetition, field recordings and modest sonic materials. The reduced default selects the synth/guitar/loop intersection while leaving their other methods editable. Unlike ambient_synth’s foregrounded arpeggio model, this branch gives diffuse melody and recorded fragments more space. Geography supports the catalogue grouping; it does not warrant adding folklore instruments, an Indigenous lineage or tango rhythm without entry-specific evidence.

entries.geo_rationale: Kompakt documents Fresco’s Buenos Aires formation and recording there; Durand’s own interview also discusses the metropolitan scene. The pin is one practice anchor, not an exclusive origin.

tradition.name: Australian ambient
tradition.lineage: Australian atmospheric electronic and electroacoustic practices, represented here by Lawrence English and the Brisbane ROOM40 network: environmental listening, recorded sound and slowly transformed electronic material. A representative field-recording/synthesis arrangement is selected rather than a national instrument inventory.

extras.description: Australian ambient groups a diverse scene by documented practice in Australia. The selected Lawrence English branch emphasizes field-recorded environments and their transformation: Ghost Towns is built largely from recorded sound treated with EQ and pitch shifting, and later collaborations credit electronics and environmental recordings. The sampler is a registered representation of recorded-material manipulation and the synth a quiet sustaining layer; neither is asserted as the hardware used on Ghost Towns. Compared with the melodic synth-and-guitar selection for Argentine ambient, this default gives listening texture and irregular environmental events greater weight. No pan-Australian timbre, automatic didgeridoo chair or Indigenous provenance is inferred.
exemplars: David Toop & Lawrence English — The Shell That Speaks the Sea (2023)

entries.geo_rationale: ROOM40 and English document Brisbane performance/label activity; the Commons photograph also identifies Brisbane. This is one established practice node in a diverse national scene.

tradition.name: Deep ambient
tradition.lineage: An overlapping ambient discovery category represented on the author map by Max Corbacho, Rudy Adrian, Dirk Serries and others. Documented examples range from electronic drones to looped electroacoustic layers. This default selects the credited synthesizer and guitar-loop sources on Steve Roach and Dirk Serries’ Low Volume Music; it is one branch of the wider listening category.

extras.description: Gradually changing sustained material forms an immersive ambient field. Low Volume Music explicitly credits Roach’s synthesizers and Serries’ guitars and looping; the default retains both sound sources. tradition.name: Drone
tradition.lineage: Sustained-tone music treats duration, closely controlled pitch and the interaction of held tones as form. Tony Conrad’s amplified violin work supplies the selected bowed-string practice model. Drone also includes electronic and other instrumental practices; this default is neither dark ambient nor a comprehensive instrument roster for all drone music.

extras.description: Long held pitches and subtle interactions among layered tones foreground sustained sound rather than harmonic progression or a beat. This bowed-string default represents Conrad’s amplified, overdubbed violin practice and uses just intonation. Other drone practices use different tunings and sources; neither darkness nor metallic distortion is a defining requirement. Continuous bowing is modeled without a sourced claim of bridge position or classical melodic ornament.

entries.geo_rationale: The museum record locates the documented Four Violins recording at the artist’s studio on Ludlow Street, New York. The pin is a rounded city-center practice anchor, not an exclusive origin or the artist’s birthplace.

tradition.name: Experimental ambient
tradition.lineage: Ambient composition treats recorded sound, acoustic resonance, noise and electronic montage as mutable material. Tim Hecker’s Ravedeath, 1972 was built from improvised pipe-organ recordings in Reykjavik and extended studio transformation in Montreal. The default models the transformed-recording stage with sampling and granular synthesis, not an assertion that Hecker used a particular sampler or granular algorithm.

extras.description: Recorded acoustic tone, noise and electronic processing form a shifting ambient composition rather than a regular beat or a prescribed mellow pad. The sample/granular roster models Hecker’s studio montage of improvised organ recordings. The acoustic pipe organ is the documented source; these catalog chairs represent its transformed recorded material and do not replace that fact with a hardware claim.

entries.geo_rationale: Hecker’s firsthand interview describes extensive Montreal studio transformation after recording a Reykjavik church organ. Montréal anchors the composition/montage stage represented by this recipe; Reykjavik remains a documented source-recording location.

tradition.name: Indian ambient
tradition.lineage: Ambient work combining Indian classical melodic instruments and contemporary electronic production also operates across the diaspora. The selected sitar-led branch follows Al Gromer Khan’s documented Vilayat Khani training and sitar/synth recordings. This grouping does not imply a single religion, an exclusively Indian production location or one compulsory raga. Performer-relative tuning avoids asserting measured interval ratios; construction and recording settings remain authored choices.

extras.description: The selected palette places ornamented sitar melody against sustained synthesizer accompaniment. Sitar Secrets documents both straight raga pieces and electronic combinations, with tabla appearing on some tracks. This default represents a spacious, percussion-free branch, rather than prescribing the complete alap–jod–jhala–gat sequence or treating all Indian ambient music as traditional concert performance.
exemplars: Prem Joshua & Manish Vyas — Water Down the Ganges (2002)

entries.geo_rationale: The artist’s own press archive identifies Al Gromer Khan as Munich-based. This diaspora practice anchor is intentional; it does not relocate the Indian classical lineage or claim that Munich originated the genre.

tradition.name: J-ambient
tradition.lineage: A broad Japanese ambient discovery grouping spanning electronic environmental composition and later studio electroacoustic work. Hiroshi Yoshimura’s GREEN documents a Tokyo home-studio FM approach; Eiko Ishibashi’s For McCoy documents a later collage practice with synthesizers, field recordings and acoustic collaborators. The default is an authored electronic subset, not a reconstruction of either album.

extras.description: The selected electronic subset uses harmonic FM layers and edited recorded sound. Its historical reference is Yoshimura’s unhurried GREEN; the original Japanese mix omitted nature effects later added for a US edition. Ishibashi’s later studio work brings together musique concrète, synthetic layers and recurring acoustic fragments. Neither traditional Japanese instruments nor environmental recordings are compulsory across these examples.

entries.geo_rationale: GREEN’s label account identifies Yoshimura’s Tokyo home studio; Ishibashi’s label profile also identifies Tokyo. This anchors documented practice rather than asserting a sole birthplace for all Japanese ambient.

tradition.name: Organic ambient
tradition.lineage: An ambient production approach that develops slowly changing, interwoven sound through recording, synthesis and processing. Projekt explicitly classifies Jeff Greinke’s Oceanic as organic ambient, while contemporary label accounts also include acoustic instruments and environmental recordings. The term does not require an acoustic ensemble: Greinke describes Oceanic as entirely sample- and synth-based. The default selects that electronic branch.

extras.description: Layered sources are transformed into evolving timbres and spatial motion. Greinke’s Oceanic uses manipulated samples and synthesizers without additional players; other contemporary label examples integrate field recordings and acoustic textures. The default therefore uses the documented electronic core rather than assuming handpan, strings or flute are mandatory. Nature-oriented ambience is represented by Steve Roach’s processed Australian outdoor recordings in Atmosphere for Dreaming.

entries.geo_rationale: Steve Roach’s album page identifies his Tucson practice and the recording’s Baja Arizona Timehouse setting. This is an evidenced exemplar anchor for a globally distributed approach, not an exclusive birthplace.

tradition.name: Polish ambient

extras.description: A regional grouping of ambient musicians working in Poland, with acoustic/electronic and field-recording approaches rather than one mandatory style. Jacaszek’s Treny combines arranged strings with quiet electronic texture; Glimmer adds harpsichord and clarinet, while Pentral uses recordings from Gothic church interiors. The selected ensemble combines these documented acoustic/electronic practices; it does not prescribe a shared Polish tuning, inherited folk ensemble or exclusive origin.

tradition.name: Pop ambient (Kompakt beat-free electronics)
tradition.lineage: Wolfgang Voigt’s Kompakt Pop Ambient compilations began in 2001 and foreground instrumental beat-free electronic atmosphere. This reverses neither the existing vocal ambient-pop category nor its song form. Piano and sample-based harmonic abstraction are documented in the 2013 edition; synthesis, build settings and recording chain are representative authored choices.

extras.description: Kompakt’s Pop Ambient compilation idiom, curated by Wolfgang Voigt from 2001: gentle, largely beat-free electronic textures and enlarged harmonic material. The 2013 edition documents sample sculpting, piano, synthetic/natural timbre boundaries and resolving drones. Rare vocal tracks exist, but the default is instrumental. This differs from ambient_pop, whose current catalog record models intimate vocal band songs, and from ambient house or ambient techno by omitting the beat-centered ensemble.

entries.geo_rationale: Cologne anchors Kompakt label practice. The label’s official Bandcamp release page lists Cologne; no exclusive birthplace claim.

tradition.name: Ritual ambient
tradition.lineage: Ceremonial ambient practice encompasses electronic production and vocal-centered ritual performance. Lustmord’s The Word as Power documents guest voices and long studio pieces; Phurpa’s performances foreground overtone chanting and ritual instruments. The selected model processes an ametrical vocal source through a sampler, without asserting one shared religion or an authentic monastic instrumentation.

extras.description: Ambient practice foregrounding ceremony, incantation and sustained vocal or electronic space. The documented Lustmord, Phurpa and Soriah examples have substantially different approaches. Lustmord’s The Word as Power credits distinct guest voices; Phurpa performs overtone chanting with ritual instruments. The default supplies voice and sampled transformation as a contemporary studio model. It does not equate the entire genre with Bön, Tibetan monastic chant, one sacred language, or one religious institution.

entries.geo_rationale: Los Angeles anchors documented Lustmord studio practice on The Word as Power; Phurpa is Moscow-based, so this pin is deliberately representative rather than universal.

tradition.name: World meditation
tradition.lineage: Cross-cultural instrumental meditation recordings combine selected acoustic timbres and studio atmosphere. Deuter’s Koyasan explicitly credits erhu, shakuhachi, tamboura and Tibetan bowls with keyboards; Nawang Khechog’s Tibetan Meditation Music combines flute with chant and sparse accents. The default models the former palette without presenting it as the traditional ensemble of any single culture.

extras.description: A functional, cross-cultural meditation-recording grouping, represented by Deuter’s Koyasan and Nawang Khechog’s Tibetan Meditation Music. Sustained electronic atmosphere surrounds slowly paced acoustic instruments; the former album documents erhu, shakuhachi, tamboura and bowls, while the latter emphasizes flute, chant and subdued rhythm. This differs from guided_meditation by providing music rather than spoken instruction, and from ritual ambient by its contemplative listening function. No clinical efficacy or shared inherited world tradition is claimed.

entries.geo_rationale: Boulder is the sourced New Earth Records creative-office/catalog circulation anchor. This labels a recorded-music practice and publishing network, not a claimed origin for the instruments or meditation.

tradition.name: Russian witch house
tradition.lineage: A Russian witch-house discovery cluster whose roster includes IC3PEAK, CHVRN, Summer Of Haze and Fraunhofer Diffraction. The selected 2010s–2020 electronic branch is represented by IC3PEAK’s contrast between floating synthesizers, heavy 808-type beats and a lead voice moving between high singing and harsher delivery.

extras.description: A dark electronic song-and-texture model centered on processed lead voice, sustained synthetic atmosphere and heavy drum-machine low end. The recipe selects the abrasive electronic branch documented around IC3PEAK’s TRRST era. It does not treat every later IC3PEAK recording as witch house: the duo’s later Coming Home explicitly moved toward guitar and live instruments. National scope does not imply one folk melody, religion or language requirement for all members.

entries.geo_rationale: IC3PEAK’s interview documents both members growing up and forming their early musical context in Moscow. This is an origin/practice anchor for the selected era, not a statement about where they currently live.

tradition.name: Polish techno

tradition.name: Deep techno
tradition.lineage: An Every Noise discovery cluster spanning melodic, atmospheric club techno. This representative branch follows Stephan Bodzin’s live interplay of an expressive monophonic synthesizer and prepared electronic percussion. The classifier label does not imply a universally agreed historical genre boundary.

extras.description: The authored arrangement foregrounds a sustained, manually inflected synth melody over a steady programmed beat. Filter movement and gradual phrase development supply motion without filling every frequency band. Bodzin’s documented Moog-centered performance is the reference, while Minimoog lineage and sample settings are catalog approximations rather than an exact Sub37 patch or a specification for the whole cluster.

entries.geo_rationale: Bodzin’s first-person production interview places his basement studio in Bremen. This is a selected production anchor, not a claimed origin for the entire discovery label.

tradition.name: Danish techno
tradition.lineage: Denmark-centered techno networks range from Kölsch’s melodic club work to the harder Copenhagen underground. This default selects the former’s documented combination of modular synthesis and drum-machine rhythm, rather than treating the national category as one tempo or mood.

extras.description: An authored melodic studio branch: arpeggiated modular tones evolve over articulated machine percussion, with spacious reverb and clear repeating phrases. The model leaves room for live adjustment rather than specifying a fixed modular patch. Rawer and faster Danish productions are part of the broader label but are not forced into this particular setup.

entries.geo_rationale: Kompakt’s artist biography documents Kölsch’s Copenhagen upbringing and production identity; this anchors the selected branch.

tradition.name: Russian techno

tradition.name: Arabic jazz
tradition.lineage: Arab-music and jazz encounters, represented by Anouar Brahem’s drummerless Thimar trio. Oud, bass clarinet and plucked double bass keep their separate voices while sharing composed melodies and improvisation. This is one branch of a much wider transnational category.

extras.description: The authored trio gives ornamented oud melody room to converse with low reed lines and a flexible bass pulse. No drum kit or compulsory piano is added. The maqam24EDO setting is only a catalog approximation to flexible modal intonation, not a claim that these musicians uniformly played equal quarter-tones. Exact woods, string brand and reed range are representative choices.

entries.geo_rationale: ECM identifies Brahem’s Tunisian training and Tunis roots; the pin marks the selected cultural anchor, while the session occurred in Oslo.

tradition.name: British jazz
tradition.lineage: Contemporary British jazz; selected London tenor-and-electric-piano quartet

extras.description: The authored Inner Game branch pairs a tenor saxophone line with reed-electric-piano harmony, plucked double bass and responsive drums. It selects the credited Wurlitzer color rather than substituting a Rhodes; acoustic piano remains an optional alternative on the source recording. The 200A, medium cane reed and clean signal path are authored realizations, not verified equipment used at the session. The catalog’s Ray Charles Wurlitzer-use selector represents a modeled soulful keyboard role, not a claim of direct stylistic influence on Garcia.

tradition.name: Dutch jazz
tradition.lineage: Contemporary Dutch jazz; selected Tineke Postma composition-led quintet

extras.description: The authored Freya branch combines alto saxophone and trumpet with piano, double bass and drums. Lyrical themes and layered group responses can open into less prescribed improvisation. Soprano saxophone and electric bass are credited alternatives, not additional simultaneous players. The saxophone model, mouthpiece, piano build and trumpet construction are representative catalog choices; this does not assert a uniform Dutch national timbre.

tradition.name: Estonian jazz
tradition.lineage: Estonia-connected jazz, represented by Kristjan Randalu’s Absence trio with electric guitarist Ben Monder and drummer Markku Ounaskari. This bassless ensemble opens carefully structured piano compositions to improvised color and interplay.

extras.description: The authored arrangement gives piano the harmonic and low-register foundation while clean guitar arpeggios add sustained color and drums articulate changing density. It does not automatically add a double bass to a documented bassless trio. Semi-hollow construction and subtle delay are chosen ways to realize the electric-guitar role; no exact Monder guitar model is asserted.

entries.geo_rationale: Randalu’s official biography gives Tallinn origin. The selected album was recorded in France, so the pin represents his Estonian roots rather than a session location.
